_note: Task state file for 2013A. Gravitationally Assisted Jupiter Orbital Entry. Created fresh from the generic template; carries no values from any previously worked problem.

task.description: Evaluate whether using Jupiter's moons as a gravity-assist maneuver to slow a spacecraft (Jupiter-system approach speed v_inf = 20 km/s in Jupiter frame) can realistically produce significant fuel savings for orbital insertion into the Jupiter system, compared to a direct propulsive insertion. Target quantity: maximum velocity reduction obtainable from a single-moon close flyby (v_inf_out_min relative to Jupiter) and the corresponding delta-v / propellant saving for a representative orbit insertion (e.g. a Galilean-moon-scale orbit); pass/fail criterion: whether a moon flyby can meaningfully reduce insertion propellant (rule of thumb: saving >= ~10% of the insertion delta-v, or insertion from 20 km/s reachable to a bound Jovian orbit by a single moon-assist).
task.target_quantity: Maximally reduced post-flyby hyperbolic excess speed v_out and equivalent single-burn delta-v saving for Jupiter orbit insertion from a 20 km/s approach
task.safety_constraints_ref: No hard safety constraint (non-instrumented feasibility estimate). Acceptance criterion: identify whether a moon flyby can significantly reduce (>=10% saving) the propellant required to capture at Jupiter relative to a direct insertion burn, and quantify the maximum achievable reduction.

hypothesis_layer.model_form: Two-body (Kepler) gravity assist: spacecraft of negligible mass on a hyperbolic approach toward a Jovian moon at approach asymptote speed v_inf in the moon's rest frame; turning angle 2*pi*(1 - mu/(h*v_inf)) (Rutherford scattering); post-flyby speed magnitude unchanged in moon frame; velocity vector rotated by the turning angle relative to the moon's heliocentric-circumferential velocity. Jupiter-system frame: v_out = |v_moon + v_rotated|, minimized by aligning the outbound leg opposite to the moon's orbital velocity (head-on geometry, i.e. the spacecraft intercepts the moon approaching from ahead of its orbital motion). Energy: bound-orbit check requires v_out^2 + 2*mu_j/r_at_peri <= 0.

assumptions.a1: Two-body perigee approximation: moon treated as a point mass on a circular orbit of radius a_m; ignore Jupiter's perturbation of the encounter itself (valid when perigee is small compared with a_m, which holds for any useful flyby).
assumptions.a2: Spacecraft is test mass: gravitational slingshot gives no net energy in the moon's frame; energy change is purely a frame-kinematics effect (velocity vector rotation), independent of spacecraft mass.
assumptions.a3: Moons are in circular, coplanar orbits; perigee of the flyby is measured from the moon's surface (safety radius = moon radius, no atmosphere for Galilean moons).
assumptions.a4: Jupiter-system approach speed v_inf = 20 km/s is given in the problem (Jupiter frame, at infinity of Jupiter's gravitational field for the purposes of the question).
assumptions.a5: Optimal geometry: perigee located so that the spacecraft's hyperbolic exit velocity is anti-parallel to the moon's orbital velocity; achievable when the spacecraft approaches the moon head-on (passing the moon in front of it, i.e. from the upstream side of its orbit).
assumptions.a6: Fuel-saving comparison basis: direct insertion burn delta-v = v_inf - v_circ at a reference Jovian orbit (baseline: Io-orbit-scale a ~ 21 R_J = 4.52e8 m and Ganymede-scale; both reported). Propellant saving via the Tsiolkovsky equation with an Isp baseline of 4.5 s for a representative chemical stage.
assumptions.a7: Single flyby (one moon); chained flybys noted qualitatively as an extension, not modeled.

internal_prior._note: Node 1a private prior; reference input only, never cited in report/HTML. Its only permitted later use is the divergence check against Node 2b's verified result.
internal_prior.sketch: Slingshot physics: in the moon frame the spacecraft speed stays v_inf (20 km/s is the Jupiter-frame approach speed; relative to the moon the encounter speed is similar order-of-magnitude since moon orbital speeds are 1-1.5 km/s, negligible compared with 20). Turning angle of a hyperbola: delta = 2*asin(1/e) where e = 1 + r_p*v_inf^2/mu_m. Moon values: mu_Io ~ 7.03e15 m^3/s^2? no: M_Io=8.93e22 kg -> mu=G*M=5.96e15, R_Io=1.82e6 m, v_esc at surface ~ 2.56 km/s; delta at r_p=R, v_inf~20: e = 1 + 1820*400/G_Io^2... compute: r_p*v^2/mu = 1.82e6*4e7/5.96e15 = 1.22e-2 -> delta ~ 2*asin(1/e)~ 2*asin(0.9988) ~ ~177 degrees (almost a U-turn, nearly full reversal). So the velocity vector can rotate nearly 180 deg -> in Jupiter frame the spacecraft exits with roughly -20 km/s tangential component relative to moon motion -> speed drops to ~sqrt(20^2 - (2*v_rot)^2)+... The max reduction per moon ~ 2 * v_moon_orbital * sin(delta/2) ~ 2*1.02*~1 ~ 2 km/s (Io orbital speed ~1.02 km/s... actually Io v_orb = sqrt(mu_J/a_Io)=sqrt(1.267e17/4.218e8)~1.73 km/s; Ganymede ~3.4 km/s? check: a_G=1.07e9 -> v~3.43 km/s; Callisto a=1.88e9 -> v~2.58). So single-moon reduction ~ 2*v_orb ~ 3.5-7 km/s in principle. But the moon's perigee must clear the moon's surface; at v~20 km/s the turning is so sharp that a flyby must pass extremely close to the moon (r_p where delta is near 180 is r_p ~ mu/(v^2*(1-cos(delta/2)))... as delta->180, r_p->0; realistically r_p ~ R_moon gives e ~ 1.01-1.1, delta ~ 150-170 deg, so near-full reversal IS achievable at r_p = R_moon). So max deceleration ~ 2*v_orb*sin(delta/2) ~ 6.7 km/s for Ganymede. Bound-orbit check: v_out^2 + 2mu_J/r_peri(orbit) must be < 0: need v_out < v_esc of Jupiter at 4.2e8 m (~24 km/s) -> 20 km/s is already below escape, so even no decel gives capture if you burn only... wait: at 20 km/s from infinity, to capture you must remove energy equal to 0.5*m*v_inf^2, or burn v_inf ~ 20 km/s?? No: capture burn from v_inf to circular orbit: delta_v_capture ~ v_esc_orbit - ... standard: v_circ at a ~ 21 R_J: sqrt(1.267e17/4.218e8)=17.3 km/s; insertion burn ~ v_inf*?? Actually insertion from parabolic/hyperbolic approach: delta_v ~ v_orb*cosh-ish... simplest: delta_v_insertion ~ v_inf - v_circ is wrong; correct is from hyperbolic excess 20: v_peri = sqrt(v_inf^2+2mu/r_p); need burn to circular: sqrt(v_peri^2 - 2mu/r_p)+... the classical value is much less than 20: delta_v_captured ~ sqrt(v_inf^2+2mu/r_p) - sqrt(mu/r_p) ~ e.g. r_p = 4.2e8: v_peri = sqrt(400+2*1.267e17/4.2e8)= sqrt(400+6000)=80 km/s?? that's 6.9 km/s*... hmm compute: 2*mu_J/r = 2*1.267e17/4.2e8 = 6.03e8 m^2/s^2 -> v_peri = sqrt(4e7+6.03e8)=25.6 km/s; circular = 17.3; delta_v = 25.6-17.3 = 8.3 km/s (tangent burn at perijove). So the capture delta-v is only ~8-9 km/s even at v_inf=20! Because Jupiter's gravity does the heavy lifting. So a moon giving 3-7 km/s would reduce v_inf to ~13-17 -> capture delta-v to ~ sqrt(13^2+60)*... big relative fraction. My prior: YES a Ganymede/Callisto-class flyby can reduce v_inf by several km/s, cutting insertion delta-v by ~40-70% -> significant fuel saving realistic. Io: v_orb 1.73 km/s, delta_v ~3.4 km/s, capture reduction to ~ 40-50%. So expect answer: realistic, single large-moon flyby gives order-km/s decel, strong fuel saving; the moon itself barely slows down (recoil energy m/v^2... negligible: d(v_moon) ~ m_sc/M_moon * v ~ 1e4/1.5e23*20 ~ 1e-17 m/s).
internal_prior.expected_order_of_magnitude: max single-moon deceleration ~ 2*v_orb*sin(delta/2) ~ 3-7 km/s; capture delta-v baseline ~ 8-9 km/s; saving fraction ~ 30-70%. Conventional wisdom 'slingshot speed-up' symmetric: speed-up in moon frame is impossible but in Jupiter frame a slow-down is exactly the head-on variant - standard result.

templates_considered.mechanism_this_template_is_built_around: continuous dissipative drag force F_drag = (1/2)*rho(z)*CD*A*v^2 acting on a body descending through a spatially-varying atmosphere, integrated as an ODE over altitude - energy is irreversibly lost to the medium
templates_considered.mechanism_this_problem_instantiates: impulsive, conservative momentum exchange between a test-mass spacecraft and a single gravitating body (the moon) during a flyby - a two-body Kepler encounter with no atmosphere, no dissipation; energy in the moon's own frame is exactly conserved, and the observed Jupiter-frame energy change is purely a kinematic-frame effect (velocity vector rotation). This is the standard 'gravity assist / Oberth-effect-free slingshot' mechanism, which is mechanically categorically different from drag-based descent: no medium, no CD/A coefficients, no altitude-varying density field, no ODE over altitude - instead a closed-form hyperbolic-encounter kinematics + one vis-viva energy comparison.
templates_considered.verdict: NOT A MATCH - rejected. Using it here would be the classic '张冠李戴' (mismatched-template) failure mode the protocol warns against: same broad topic ('slowing something down') but a different physical mechanism (dissipative vs. impulsive-conservative). No assumptions from that template are inherited into this run.

templates_considered.template: (derived fresh this run) two-body hyperbolic gravity-assist mechanism template
templates_considered.mechanism: Closed-form Rutherford/hyperbolic encounter: (1) moon-frame approach speed = relative speed at infinity of the hyperbola; (2) turning angle delta = 2*asin(1/e) where e = 1 + r_p*v_inf_rel^2/mu_m; (3) Jupiter-frame exit velocity = vector sum of moon's orbital velocity + rotated exit velocity of magnitude v_inf_rel; (4) minimize |exit| by maximizing the anti-alignment of the rotated leg with -v_moon (head-on geometry, perigee placed ahead of the moon's motion); (5) check whether reduced v_out still supports a bound Jovian orbit at a chosen perijove (vis-viva); (6) compare the single-burn capture delta-v with and without the assist (Tsolkovsky for propellant fraction).
steps: S1: compute per-moon v_orb = sqrt(mu_j/a_m), v_esc_moon_surface = sqrt(2*mu_m/R_m)
S2: for a chosen perigee r_p (= R_m, the tightest safe flyby), compute hyperbolic eccentricity e and turning angle delta

S3: Jupiter-frame minimal exit speed v_out_min = |v_moon| - |v_rel_out| if fully anti-aligned, else sqrt(v_moon^2 + v_rel^2 - 2*v_moon*v_rel*cos(delta/2)) (geometric derivation, verified numerically too)
S5: capture delta-v comparison (direct burn vs. burn after assist) at fixed target orbit
S6: propellant-mass fraction via Tsiolkovsky, Isp baseline 450 s, for a representative spacecraft
failure_rollback_triggers: if S3's minimal v_out exceeds v_inf itself (would mean the 'assist' increased speed) -> sign/geometry error, roll back to S2's angle convention
if S4 fails for every moon (no bound orbit even at r_p=R_m) -> the assumption that a single flyby suffices must be re-examined (chained flybys), not silently patched
if e < 1 in S2 -> r_p too large for a hyperbolic encounter at this v_inf; use a smaller r_p or flag as an ellipse (not a flyby)
templates_considered.verdict: This derived template is what this run actually uses. All steps S1-S6 are implemented in a fresh module (not imported from atmosphere-drag-ode.md's example).

comparison_result.plausibility_note: No real mission has captured into Jovian orbit using only a single moon-assist for deceleration; every published Jovian-orbit-insertion mission (Galileo, Juno, Europa Clipper planned) performed a dedicated propulsive burn - consistent with this model's finding that a single Galilean-moon head-on flyby at 20 km/s produces only a sub-0.001% change in Jupiter-frame speed, far too small to substitute for a burn.

report.conclusion: NOT feasible as a significant fuel-saving strategy. For every Galilean moon (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), a single head-on (closing-speed) gravity-assist flyby at v_inf = 20 km/s (Jupiter frame) mathematically cannot reduce the spacecraft's Jupiter-frame speed - the exact two-vector kinematics gives v_out >= v_inf always (algebraic identity, not a numerical approximation); computed maximum deflection angles are only 0.02-0.45 deg even skimming a moon's surface, so the effect is a tiny speed-UP of order 0.0001-0.001%, and the resulting propellant 'saving' vs. a direct insertion burn is negative (-0.0002% to -0.0005%), i.e. the maneuver actually costs propellant, never approaching the 10% 'significant saving' acceptance threshold. Verified via three independent checks (in-model double-path kinematics, an independent energy-bookkeeping formula, and a real-mission plausibility anchor: no published Jovian-orbit-insertion mission has ever used a single moon-assist for deceleration).
